prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. After the full first-round exchange the argument is, if anything, sharper. The 2011 continuum-model calculation made a quantitative, falsifiable statement (the lowest moire bands flatten at a small discrete set of twist angles), and the 2018 experiments found correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. This is theory-led discovery of the kind I most value as a condensed-matter theorist, and it is checkable: the continuum band structure has been compared with scanning-tunnelling spectroscopy, transport and DFT-based tight-binding calculations, and the phase diagram has been reproduced by many independent groups and carried into other van der Waals moire platforms. The chair asked which parts are settled enough to cite without a pairing mechanism: the flat bands, the correlated insulating states and the existence of superconductivity at the magic angle. The citation I propose rests only on those and says nothing about the origin of pairing. Four members now share this configuration with the same three names, and every one of them would keep Bistritzer, which is as settled as a laureate list gets. I also want to be clear that the clock is a worthy rival and I would not be unhappy with it; my preference rests on discovery of a new regime rather than on counting support.
statement.case_against: The unsettled pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variability are real, and the attribution is imperfect: Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto identified reduced bandwidth at small angles earlier, and Cao, Fatemi and other co-first authors and Cory Dean's group fall outside a three-name limit. A committee that insists the interpretation be finished, or that every experimental contributor be named, would find the optical lattice clock (B049) the cleaner and more finished case, with two names that nobody disputes. The risk that a later result such as the fractional Chern insulator looks more elegant in hindsight is also real, although I do not think it should displace the original discovery.

responses.point: Kroll lists B009 as his second alternative and asks whether the correlated-state phase diagram is as reproducible between groups as the clock comparisons are, saying that a yes would largely remove his maturity hesitation and leave only the experimental attribution.
responses.response: I can answer partly, as a theorist who follows the data but does not make the samples. The existence of the correlated insulator near half filling and of superconducting domes near the magic angle has been reproduced by several independent groups, and the broad topology of the phase diagram is robust. What is not as reproducible as a clock comparison is the fine detail: critical temperatures, which fillings show superconductivity, and the dependence on twist-angle homogeneity differ between devices, and that is why I want the citation limited to the existence of the states and not their parameters. That is a weaker standard than an agreement at the 1e-18 level, and I will not pretend otherwise. But the discovery claim does not rest on the parameters. On experimental attribution, the honest position is that a three-name limit forces a choice, and the person who led the programme and whose laboratory the community recognises as the origin is the defensible one.

responses.point: Pearce, whose own preferred configuration is B049 and who lists B009 as his first alternative, asks which part of the discovery is settled enough to cite without the pairing mechanism, and notes the attribution questions around Cao, Dean's group and earlier flat-band theory.
responses.response: Your question is the right one and I have tried to answer it in the wording of the citation: the prediction of flat bands at magic angles, and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states. Nothing in that wording needs a pairing mechanism. I would ask the committee to look at it the way we looked at graphene in 2010: nobody then needed to understand every consequence of the new material for the discovery to be recognised. On attribution I do not think the Lopes dos Santos work removes the Bistritzer-MacDonald claim, because the quantitative magic-angle condition is what the experiments tested; but I agree with you and with Mehlig that the committee should confirm this in the primary literature before the vote, and if that check shows a priority problem I would say so openly rather than defend the trio out of habit.

responses.point: Mehlig, who moved to B009 as his first choice, wants the citation to credit the specific magic-angle statement and not an earlier general observation of flat-band signatures, and warns that the committee can only defend what it can check.
responses.response: I agree and I have adopted that framing: the citation says prediction of flat bands at magic angles, which is the quantitative claim. In my first-round reply I asked about B026 and you did not answer, so I will drop the question and state my own view: I keep topological insulators as an alternative but I have not seen a reason to rank them above B009, because the quantised-conductance and materials-quality questions you raised for them are not matched by a comparable doubt about the existence of the states in magic-angle graphene. Your point about the fractional Chern insulator I read as an argument for a later, separate recognition, as I did in round one.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the lattice clock first but states that he would not oppose B009 if the condensed-matter members are confident, while noting the unsettled interpretation and the earlier flat-band claim.
responses.response: I am confident in the part of the claim that matters for a prize: the states exist, are reproducible in their essentials, and appear where the prediction said they should. I am not confident about the pairing mechanism, and I do not think we should pretend to be. As to the clock, I accept your argument that the many-atom lattice gives a statistical gain that single ions cannot match, so I no longer describe it as only a refinement of the Wineland clock; that is a change from my first-round reply. Where we still differ is in what counts as a discovery. For me a result that reveals a new regime in nature carries more weight than record precision, even a very good one, but I recognise that this is a judgment about the prize rather than a fact, and I would not call the clock a mistake.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder as reasons to wait, or the flat bands plus correlated and superconducting states as a complete discovery.
Whether the primary literature supports crediting Bistritzer and MacDonald over Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto for the magic-angle prediction; I have not verified the priority record myself.
Whether leaving out Cao, Fatemi, other co-first authors and Dean's group can be defended within three names; I think so but I hold it with less confidence than the theory attribution.
I cannot independently judge priority questions in the lattice clock lineage (Lemonde, Hollberg, single-ion clocks) and defer to the atomic physicists on whether the two-name B049 list is complete.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I know of no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, nor to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. My work on electronic structure, DFT codes and atomistic spin dynamics at Uppsala is in the same broad field as moire materials, which is a source of expertise and of possible bias toward theory-led condensed-matter discoveries, not a personal conflict. I note Kroll's disclosure on the JILA group and Johansson's on circuit QED and have no objection to either as stated.
